title: Chemical Reactions: Combination and Decomposition
summary: What a chemical reaction is, its signs, and the combination and decomposition types with equations and uses.

p: A chemical reaction is a process in which substances (reactants) change into new substances (products) with different composition and properties. In it, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds are formed. Example: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l).

Signs of a chemical reaction: a gas is given off; a colour change; heat or light is given out or taken in; a precipitate (solid) forms. Other features: there is always an energy change; mass is conserved (the law of conservation of mass); many reactions cannot easily be reversed.
Everyday examples: cooking food, burning fuel, rusting of iron, photosynthesis.
Reactions can be grouped as combination, decomposition and displacement (and others, such as neutralisation and redox, which you have met). This unit covers the first two.
Two or more simple substances join to form one product: A + B → AB.

Examples: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s) (magnesium burns with a bright white flame, leaving white ash). C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g). N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) (Haber process). CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) (making slaked lime, used in cement and to treat acid soil).
Features: usually exothermic (give out heat) and only one product. Uses: burning fuels for energy, making ammonia for fertiliser, cement.

Note: the source notes give photosynthesis as an example of combination. Photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) is not a simple one-product combination and is endothermic, as it takes in energy from sunlight, so we do not treat it as a typical combination reaction. Also, not every combination reaction is exothermic (N₂ + O₂ → 2NO takes in heat).
One compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances: AB → A + B. Usually energy must be supplied (endothermic).
Thermal decomposition (by heat): CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); 2KClO₃(s) → 2KCl(s) + 3O₂(g) (with MnO₂ as a catalyst; used to prepare oxygen in the laboratory).
Electrolytic decomposition (by electricity): 2H₂O(l) → 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) (by electrolysis).
Photolytic decomposition (by light): 2AgCl(s) → 2Ag(s) + Cl₂(g). This is why silver salts are kept in dark bottles and why photographic film is kept away from light.
Uses: preparing gases in the laboratory, making lime from limestone, electrolysis, photography. Decomposition of food by microbes leads to spoilage.

title: Displacement Reactions and the Reactivity Series
summary: How a more reactive element displaces a less reactive one, with metals and halogens, the reactivity series, and uses such as galvanising.

p: In a displacement reaction a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound: A + BC → AC + B.

Examples: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s): zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper (the blue solution fades and brown copper forms). Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s): iron displaces copper (an iron nail in copper sulphate becomes coated with copper). Cl₂(g) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq): chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine (the solution turns orange).
The reverse reactions do not happen: copper does not displace zinc from zinc sulphate, because copper is less reactive than zinc.
The reactivity series lists metals from the most reactive to the least reactive. A metal higher in the list can displace one lower in the list from its compound.

img.alt: A vertical list of metals from potassium at the top, most reactive, through sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver to gold at the bottom, least reactive

p: Extraction of metals: carbon displaces (reduces) iron from its oxide, Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, because carbon is more reactive than iron in a furnace. Galvanising: iron is coated with zinc; even if scratched the zinc, being more reactive, reacts first, so the iron does not rust. Recovering metals: copper can be recovered from solution by adding scrap iron. Water purification: halogen displacement and the reactions of chlorine.
Predicting: will Fe react with CuSO₄? Yes (iron is above copper). Will Cu react with ZnSO₄? No. Will Mg react with HCl? Yes (magnesium is above hydrogen), giving hydrogen and magnesium chloride.

title: Energy Changes: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions
summary: How reactions give out or take in energy, enthalpy change ΔH, activation energy and energy profile diagrams.

p: Every chemical reaction involves a change of energy. Energy may appear as heat, light, sound or electricity. Energy can be given out to the surroundings or taken in from them. Knowing this helps us to predict whether a reaction will go, to explain temperature changes and to use chemical energy in industry, in living things and in the home.
An exothermic reaction gives out heat (or other energy) to the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter. Example: burning methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat.
An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder. Example: thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heat is taken in).
1. Conservation of energy: energy is never created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. In a reaction, energy passes between the reacting substances and their surroundings.
2. Enthalpy change (ΔH): the heat change of a reaction at constant pressure. ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions (energy released) and positive for endothermic reactions (energy absorbed).

3. Activation energy (Eₐ): even exothermic reactions need a minimum energy to start, to break the first bonds in the reactants. A match must be struck before it burns, even though burning is exothermic.

Energy changes come from bond breaking and bond making: breaking bonds takes in energy; making bonds gives out energy. If more energy is given out in making bonds than is taken in to break bonds, the reaction is exothermic.

In an exothermic reaction the reactants are higher in energy than the products. The energy difference is released, and ΔH is negative. In an endothermic reaction, the products are higher in energy than the reactants, the difference is absorbed, and ΔH is positive. In both cases, there is an energy 'hill', the activation energy, between the reactants and the products.

title: Examples, Uses and Comparison of Energy Changes
summary: Characteristics and examples of exothermic and endothermic changes, simple experiments, real-life uses and a comparison table.

p: Heat is given out and the surroundings become warmer. ΔH is negative. The products are more stable (lower in energy) than the reactants. Examples: combustion of fuels (methane, propane, petrol); respiration, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy; neutralisation, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O + heat; freezing of water, which gives out heat as ice forms; adding quicklime to water; dissolving sodium hydroxide in water.

Heat is taken in and the surroundings become colder. ΔH is positive. The products are higher in energy than the reactants. They often need a continuous supply of energy. Examples: photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + sunlight → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate; dissolving ammonium chloride in water; electrolysis of water, 2H₂O + energy → 2H₂ + O₂; melting ice (a change of state that takes in heat).

title: Rates of Reaction and the Factors That Affect Them
summary: What the rate of reaction is, how to measure it, and how concentration, temperature, pressure, surface area, the nature of the reactants and light change it.

sections.h: What is the rate of a reaction?
p: The rate of reaction is how fast reactants are changed into products. It tells us how much reactant is used or how much product is formed in a given time. Rate = change in concentration of a reactant (or product) ÷ time taken. Units: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ for concentration, cm³ s⁻¹ for the volume of gas given off, or g s⁻¹ for a change in mass.

Gas given off: collect the gas in a gas syringe or an upturned measuring cylinder (for example, magnesium with hydrochloric acid). Loss of mass: put the flask on a balance and watch the mass fall as gas escapes (marble chips with acid). Colour change: watch the colour fade or appear. Cloudiness: time how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear as a precipitate forms (sodium thiosulphate with hydrochloric acid gives sulphur).

1. Nature of the reactants: ionic reactions in solution, such as HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, are very fast because the ions are already free. Reactions that must break strong covalent bonds, such as methane with chlorine, are slow unless there is light or heat.

2. Concentration: a higher concentration means more particles in the same volume, so more collisions each second, so a faster reaction. 2 mol/dm³ HCl reacts with magnesium faster than 0.5 mol/dm³ HCl. On a graph of volume of gas against time, the curve is steeper.

3. Temperature: a higher temperature gives the particles more energy, so they move faster, collide more often, and more of the collisions have enough energy to react. As a rough rule, the rate about doubles for every 10 °C rise. Food spoils faster in warm weather and lasts longer in a refrigerator.
4. Pressure (for gases): raising the pressure squeezes gas particles closer together, so there are more collisions. The Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, uses high pressure.

5. Surface area: a reaction takes place at the surface of a solid. Powder has a larger surface than lumps, so it reacts faster. Powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster with acid than marble chips; sawdust burns faster than a log; flour dust can explode.

6. Light: some reactions are speeded up or started by light (photochemical reactions), for example photosynthesis, 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, and the decomposition of silver halides in photography, 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂.
7. A catalyst (see the next unit).

title: Collision Theory, Catalysts and Industrial Uses
summary: Why particles must collide effectively, how catalysts lower the activation energy, the types of catalysis, and how rate ideas are used in industry.

p: For a reaction to happen, particles must collide; the collision must be effective, meaning they hit with the right orientation and with enough energy; and the minimum energy needed is the activation energy (Eₐ). Most collisions are not effective. Anything that increases the number of effective collisions per second raises the rate.

A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up or permanently changed. It works by providing a different path with a lower activation energy, so more particles have enough energy to react. A catalyst does not change the products or the total energy released.

Examples: manganese(IV) oxide, MnO₂, catalyses the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water (2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂). Iron catalyses the Haber process. Nickel catalyses the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make margarine. Enzymes are the catalysts of living things.

img.alt: An energy profile with a high hill for the uncatalysed reaction and a lower hill for the catalysed reaction, between the same reactants and products
img.cap: A catalyst lowers the activation energy.

p: Homogeneous catalysis: the catalyst is in the same state as the reactants (for example, nitrogen monoxide gas catalysing the oxidation of sulphur dioxide gas in an older process). Heterogeneous catalysis: the catalyst is in a different state (solid iron in the gaseous Haber process). Autocatalysis: one of the products speeds up the reaction (in the hydrolysis of an ester, the acid produced acts as catalyst).

Concentration: magnesium with hydrochloric acid of different concentrations; measure the hydrogen given off. Temperature: sodium thiosulphate with hydrochloric acid at different temperatures; time the disappearance of a cross. Catalyst: hydrogen peroxide with and without manganese(IV) oxide; collect the oxygen. Surface area: calcium carbonate powder and marble chips with acid.

Haber process (ammonia): iron catalyst, about 200 atmospheres pressure and 450 °C: a high enough temperature for a good rate, without losing too much ammonia. Contact process (sulphuric acid): vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, about 450 °C. Hydrogenation of oils: nickel catalyst to make margarine. Polymerisation: catalysts control the rate and the yield of plastics. In all industries the aim is to make products quickly and cheaply and with little waste.

title: Reversible Reactions and Chemical Equilibrium
summary: Irreversible and reversible reactions, what dynamic equilibrium is, and what happens to the concentrations over time.

p: An irreversible reaction goes in one direction only, from reactants to products, and the products cannot easily change back. Examples: burning methane, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; neutralisation, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.

A reversible reaction can go in both directions under the same conditions. It is shown by a double arrow ⇌. Examples: the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); heating calcium carbonate in a closed vessel, CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), where the products can recombine; heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate gives white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate and water, and adding water changes it back to blue (a test for water).

In a reversible reaction carried out in a closed system, the forward and backward reactions both happen until a state called dynamic equilibrium is reached. At equilibrium: the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction; the concentrations of the reactants and products stay constant (they are not necessarily equal); and the system is dynamic: the reactions still go on, but there is no overall change.
In the Haber process, at first the formation of NH₃ is fast. As NH₃ builds up, it decomposes back to N₂ and H₂ faster, until the two rates are equal.

img.alt: A graph of concentration against time: the concentrations of nitrogen and hydrogen fall and the concentration of ammonia rises until all three become constant at equilibrium
img.cap: Concentrations change until equilibrium is reached, then stay constant.

p: The same equilibrium mixture is reached whether we start with N₂ and H₂ or start with NH₃, provided the conditions are the same. This is shown by the two graphs in many textbooks: starting with reactants, the reactants fall and the product rises; starting with the product, the product falls and the reactants rise; in both cases the concentrations level off.

title: Le Chatelier's Principle and the Equilibrium Constant
summary: How changes in concentration, pressure, temperature and catalyst affect an equilibrium, the equilibrium constant Kc with a calculation, and the Haber and Contact processes.

p: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure or temperature, the system shifts in the direction that opposes the change and tries to restore balance.

Adding more reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products. Adding more product shifts it towards the reactants. In N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, adding more H₂ moves the equilibrium to the right (more NH₃); adding NH₃ moves it to the left. Removing NH₃ as it is formed moves it to the right, which is what is done in industry.

Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules; lowering the pressure favours the side with more gas molecules. In N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. High pressure moves the equilibrium to the right (more NH₃).

For a reaction that is exothermic in the forward direction, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium backward (towards the reactants) and lowering the temperature shifts it forward. For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature shifts it forward. The Haber reaction is exothermic: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat, so a high temperature gives less ammonia.
A catalyst speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally. It lets the system reach equilibrium sooner but does not change the position of equilibrium or the amount of product at equilibrium.

For the reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, at a fixed temperature: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ ([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ), where the square brackets mean concentration in mol/dm³. A large Kc means that products are favoured at equilibrium; a small Kc means reactants are favoured. Kc changes only with temperature.

Example: for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³). At equilibrium, [NH₃] = 0.2, [N₂] = 0.1 and [H₂] = 0.3 mol/dm³. Kc = 0.2² ÷ (0.1 × 0.3³) = 0.04 ÷ (0.1 × 0.027) = 0.04 ÷ 0.0027 = 14.8 (units mol⁻² dm⁶).

Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic): high pressure (about 200 atmospheres) favours the forward reaction; a moderate temperature (about 450 °C) is a compromise, because a lower temperature gives more ammonia but too slowly; iron with promoters is the catalyst; ammonia is liquefied and removed, and unreacted gas is recycled.

Contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic, ΔH about −197 kJ per mole of O₂): a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst; a temperature of about 450 °C as a compromise. High pressure would favour SO₃ (3 moles to 2), but the yield is already high at about 1 to 2 atmospheres, so very high pressure is not worth the cost. (The source notes say 'high pressure and low temperature'. That favours the forward reaction in theory, but in practice, moderate conditions are chosen.)
In the body, oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood follow equilibrium ideas, and Le Chatelier's principle helps to explain gas exchange in the lungs.

For CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH (forward exothermic; 3 moles of gas to 1): raising the pressure gives more methanol; lowering the temperature gives more methanol; adding a catalyst does not change the yield, it only reaches equilibrium faster.

title: Metals and Non-Metals: Properties
summary: Where metals and non-metals are found in the periodic table, their physical and chemical properties, metalloids and a comparison table.

p: Elements are grouped as metals and non-metals according to their properties. Metals are on the left and in the centre of the periodic table; non-metals are on the right. A staircase line separates them. They form the materials of industry, farming, building, medicine and technology.
Metals readily lose electrons to form positive ions (cations) and have metallic bonding.

Physical properties: malleable (can be hammered into sheets, like aluminium foil); ductile (can be drawn into wires, like copper); good conductors of heat and electricity because of free (delocalised) electrons; most have high melting and boiling points (mercury is a liquid at room temperature, and Group 1 metals melt at low temperatures); high density; shiny when polished (metallic lustre); sonorous (ring when struck); strong; can form alloys (brass, bronze, steel).

Chemical properties: they lose electrons easily (electropositive); they form basic oxides, 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O (some oxides are amphoteric, such as aluminium oxide); they react with water to differing degrees (sodium violently, calcium more slowly, gold not at all); most react with dilute acids to give a salt and hydrogen (except copper, mercury, silver, gold and platinum); they form chlorides, 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl; they form ionic compounds.
Non-metals tend to gain or share electrons, forming negative ions or covalent compounds.

Physical properties: poor conductors of heat and electricity (graphite is an exception); low melting and boiling points; many are gases or brittle solids; not malleable or ductile; usually low density; dull, with no metallic lustre; brittle; they exist in all three states (oxygen is a gas, bromine a liquid, sulphur a solid); some have allotropes (carbon as diamond and graphite, oxygen as O₂ and O₃).

Chemical properties: they gain or share electrons (electronegative); their oxides are acidic, for example CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; they form covalent compounds with hydrogen (HCl, CH₄); with metals they form ionic compounds (NaCl); across a period, non-metal reactivity generally increases.

Metalloids have properties between those of metals and non-metals. Examples: boron, silicon, arsenic, antimony and tellurium. Many are semiconductors, so silicon is used in electronics and computer chips.

title: Extraction and Uses of Metals and Non-Metals
summary: How metals are got from their ores (electrolysis, reduction with carbon, roasting), the uses of metals and non-metals, and the role of recycling.

p: Most metals are found in the ground as ores, rocks that contain a metal compound in enough amounts to be worth mining. The method of extraction depends on how reactive the metal is.

1. Electrolysis: very reactive metals such as aluminium, sodium and potassium. Aluminium is obtained from bauxite. The bauxite is first purified to give aluminium oxide (alumina). The alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite (to lower the melting point to about 950 °C) and electrolysed using carbon electrodes. Molten aluminium collects at the cathode and oxygen is released at the anode, which slowly burns away the carbon anodes. This needs a great deal of electricity.

2. Reduction with carbon (or carbon monoxide): metals of medium reactivity such as iron and zinc. Iron is extracted from haematite (iron(III) oxide) in a blast furnace: carbon burns to make carbon monoxide, which reduces the iron oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone is added to remove impurities as slag.

3. Roasting and smelting: for sulphide ores, the ore is first roasted in air to give the oxide, which is then reduced. 4. Unreactive metals like gold may occur uncombined in nature (native metals) and need only to be separated from rock.

Iron (as steel): construction, tools and machines. Copper: electrical wiring and plumbing. Aluminium: aircraft, packaging, cooking pots. Gold and silver: jewellery and electronics. Zinc: galvanising and dry-cell batteries. Lead: car batteries and shielding against radiation. Titanium: aircraft and medical implants.

Oxygen: breathing, welding, steel making. Nitrogen: fertilisers, refrigeration (liquid nitrogen), explosives. Sulphur: making sulphuric acid and vulcanising rubber. Chlorine: disinfecting water, making PVC. Carbon: fuel, steel making, graphite in pencils and lubricants, diamond in jewellery and cutting tools. Phosphorus: matches, fertilisers, detergents.

Metals and non-metals are vital for transport, medicine, communication, power and building. Recycling metals such as aluminium and iron saves energy and ore and reduces pollution; recycling aluminium uses only a small fraction of the energy needed to extract new aluminium. Waste plastics and toxic gases from non-metals must be disposed of properly to protect the environment.
